rewritten_text:
She studied me closely for a moment, then asked quietly:

‘What do you want me to do for them?’

‘Only,’ I said, ‘that you won't judge them by the others. They may be related, but believe me, they are very different people.’

Still watching me closely, Miss Havisham repeated:

‘What do you want me to do for them?’

‘As you can see,’ I replied, feeling myself blush slightly, ‘I'm not clever enough to hide the fact that I do want something, even if I tried. Miss Havisham, if you could spare the money to give my friend Herbert some lasting help in life, I could explain how. But because of the circumstances, it would have to be done without his knowing.’

‘Why must he not know?’ she asked, resting her hands on her walking stick so that she could study me more carefully.

‘Because I started helping him myself more than two years ago, without telling him, and I don't want him to find out. I can't explain why I am no longer able to finish what I began. That is part of someone else's secret, and it isn't mine to tell.’

Slowly she turned her eyes away from me and toward the fire. She stared into it for what seemed, in the silence and the light of the gradually burning candles, a very long time. The collapse of a few glowing coals brought her back to herself. She looked at me again, blankly at first, then with growing attention. Estella kept knitting throughout. Once Miss Havisham had focused on me, she spoke as though there had been no pause in our conversation:

‘What else?’

‘Estella,’ I said, turning to her and trying to steady my shaking voice, ‘you know I love you. You know I've loved you deeply for a long time.’

She raised her eyes to my face. Her fingers continued their work, and her expression showed no emotion. I noticed Miss Havisham looking from me to her and back again.

‘I would have said this sooner, but I misunderstood things for so long. My mistake led me to hope that Miss Havisham intended us to marry. While I thought you had no choice in the matter, I held back. But now I have to say it.’

Still knitting, her expression unchanged, Estella shook her head.

‘I know,’ I said in response. ‘I know. I have no hope of ever calling you mine, Estella.’

‘If it is wanted for use at home, however, I can furnish an admirable article and promise you will find the outcome satisfactory. Might I inquire who is to receive it? If you mean it for a policeman, or anyone associated with Scotland Yard, I fear I can be of no service. English detectives are in truth our closest allies; I have invariably found that their stupidity allows us to do precisely as we please. I could not bear to lose a single one.’

‘I give you my assurance,’ Lord Arthur replied, ‘that the police have nothing whatever to do with this. The clock is, in fact, meant for the Dean of Chichester.’

‘Good gracious! I never suspected you of such strong religious feelings, Lord Arthur. They are uncommon among young men these days.’

‘I fear you think too highly of me, Herr Winckelkopf,’ said Lord Arthur, colouring. ‘In truth, theology is a subject I know absolutely nothing about.’

‘A wholly personal affair, then?’

‘Wholly personal.’

With a shrug, Herr Winckelkopf went out. A few minutes later he reappeared carrying a circular piece of dynamite roughly as large as a penny and a charming little French clock. On top stood a gilded-bronze figure of Liberty crushing the hydra of Despotism beneath her feet.

At the sight, Lord Arthur's expression brightened. ‘Precisely what I wanted!’ he exclaimed. ‘Now explain to me how it explodes.’

‘Ah, that is my secret,’ replied Herr Winckelkopf, surveying his invention with well-earned pride. ‘Tell me the time you require the explosion, and I shall adjust the mechanism to the exact moment.’

‘Well, it is Tuesday today. If you could dispatch it immediately—’

‘Quite impossible. I have a great quantity of urgent work for friends in Moscow. Tomorrow, however, I might manage to send it.’

‘That will be soon enough,’ Lord Arthur said courteously, ‘provided it arrives tomorrow evening or Thursday morning. As for the explosion, let us say Friday at precisely noon. The Dean is invariably home then.’

‘Friday at noon,’ Herr Winckelkopf echoed, entering the instruction in a large ledger on a desk beside the fireplace.

‘And now,’ said Lord Arthur, getting to his feet, ‘please tell me what I owe you.’

‘The affair is so trifling, Lord Arthur, that I would rather charge nothing. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and delivery about five shillings. It is a pleasure to assist any friend of Count Rouvaloff.’

‘But what of your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?’

She suddenly wanted very much to go to the front door and see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of wanting anything else? Captain Wentworth must have disappeared from view by now. She rose from her chair, determined to go. One half of her mind should not always claim to be wiser than the other, or accuse it of motives worse than its real ones. She would check the rain. A moment later, however, Captain Wentworth himself came in and sent her back to her seat. He was with several men and women who were clearly friends of his, and whom he must have met just below Milsom Street. Seeing her plainly startled and confused him more than she had ever noticed before. He blushed deeply. For the first time since they had met again, she felt she was showing less emotion than he was. Those last few moments had given her an advantage by preparing her. The first overwhelming shock, the surprise that blinded and bewildered her, had already passed. Even so, she still felt a great deal: agitation, pain, pleasure, something between joy and misery.

He spoke to her, then turned away. Above all, his manner showed embarrassment. She could not confidently call it cold or friendly; embarrassed was the only word she was sure of.

After a short pause, he approached and spoke again. They asked each other ordinary questions, though neither probably learned much from the answers. Anne remained keenly aware that he was less comfortable than before. Having spent so much time together, they had learned to speak with an appearance of calm indifference. Now he could no longer manage it. Either time had changed him, or Louisa had. He was clearly conscious of something. He looked very well, as though neither his health nor his spirits had suffered. He talked about Uppercross and the Musgroves, and even about Louisa. When he mentioned her, his face briefly took on its familiar teasing, meaningful expression. Still, this was Captain Wentworth feeling uncomfortable and uneasy, unable even to pretend otherwise.

Anne was not surprised that Elizabeth refused to acknowledge him, but it hurt her. She saw that he noticed Elizabeth and that Elizabeth noticed him. Each had certainly recognized the other. Anne was sure he was ready to be greeted as an acquaintance, even expecting it. She had to watch her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple's carriage, which Miss Elliot had been waiting for with growing impatience, now arrived. The servant came inside to announce it.
